rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At God’s command, Ezra restores an Israelite woman’s sight and legs; she recognizes him, and the community verifies his identity by a birthmark.
rows.anchor: فقامت صحيحة كأنما نشطت من عقال فنظرت فقالت : أشهد أنك عزير فانطلقت إلى محله بنى إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites say Ezra alone retained the Torah after Nebuchadnezzar burned it; his father had hidden a copy, which Ezra retrieves as two lights enter his chest and restore his memory.
rows.anchor: لم يكن فينا أحد حفظ التوراة فيما حدثنا غير عزير وقد حرق بختنصر التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternate report says Ezra recites the Torah perfectly from memory; a descendant of captives then finds his ancestor’s hidden copy, and their texts agree, prompting the claim that Ezra is God’s son.
rows.anchor: قرأها عليهم حين طلبوا منه ذلك عن ظهر قلب من غير أن يخرم منها حرفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites’ claim that Ezra is God’s son is repudiated as utterly transcending divine truth.
rows.anchor: فعند ذلك قالوا : ﴿ عزير ابن الله ﴾ تعالى عن ذلك علوا كبيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No compulsion can produce religion’s real guidance: it is the heart’s light, inherent in human nature.
rows.anchor: لأنه في الحقيقة هو الهدى المستفاد من النور القلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right path is unity, while error consists in attending to other-than-God; the true witness of faith grasps the unbreakable bond of essential unity.
rows.anchor: الذي هو طريق الوحدة وتميز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here taghut means whatever is other than God; real, witnessed faith in God grips the essential unity that contains all possibilities.
rows.anchor: وهو ما سرى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone guides believers out of ego, fantasy, and illusion into certainty, guidance, and the spacious realm of spirits.
rows.anchor: ظلمات النفس وشبه الخيال والوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers’ attachment to otherness lets false patrons divert them from innate guidance into egoic qualities, doubts, and the fire of nature.
rows.anchor: نور الاستعداد والهداية الفطرية إلى ظلمات صفات النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputant may be Nimrod, the commanding soul that argues against Abraham’s sacred spirit; the granted kingdom symbolizes bodily powers and this low world, or the account is historical.
rows.anchor: وهو نمروذ النفس الأمارة الجادلة لإبراهيم الروح القدسية التى ألقيت في نار الطبيعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham can signify the spirit or the historical patriarch; Nimrod’s claim to give life and death allegorizes diverting powers into pleasure or temporarily withholding them, alongside pardon and killing.
rows.anchor: نمروذ النفس الامارة أو الجبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brings the sun of gnosis from its eastern source; the demand to bring it from the west either tests Nimrod or asks the spirit to return after setting in the body.
rows.anchor: من مشرقها ) وهو جانب المبدأ الفياض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passerby may be the human intellect crossing the heart, its holy house, or the prophet Ezra; the city is empty of helpful manifestations and collapsed through weak spiritual readiness.
rows.anchor: أو هو عزير النبي وكان قدم على بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about reviving the dead city expresses bewilderment at truth while ignorant and turned toward otherness; the city may also be a ruined physical place.
rows.anchor: لذهوله عن النظر إلى الحقائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hundred-year death may mean prolonged ignorance, a period of eight years and four months or twenty-five years, ascetic death during spiritual discipline, or literal natural death followed by resurrection.
rows.anchor: أبقاه جاهلا مئة عام أي مدة طويلة وقيل : هى عبارة في الأصل عن ثمانية أعوام وأربعة أشهر أو خمسة وعشرين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent short day or part of a day reflects how the period of ignorance or spiritual discipline shrinks beside eternal life; in truth he remained one hundred years.
rows.anchor: فما ظنها : إلا يوما أو بعض يوم استصغارا لمدة اللبث في موت الجهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fig symbolizes universal intelligibles, with particulars latent like its seeds; grapes symbolize particular cognition with material adjuncts, while grape juice signifies love and gnosis and milk beneficial revealed knowledge.
rows.anchor: الأول إشارة إلى المدركات الكلية لكونه لبا كله وكون الجزئيات فيه بالقوة كالحبات التى في التين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unchanged food and drink symbolize innate knowledge deposited according to each soul’s capacity: material veils may hide it, but do not erase it, and it reappears when lifted.
rows.anchor: فإن العلوم مخزونة في كل نفس بحسب استعداده الناس معادن كمعادن الذهب والفضة وإن حجبت بالمواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The donkey can signify the bodily form carrying the heart, or the outward meaning; bones are powers raised from nature and clothed with growing flesh of gnosis nourished by spiritual witnessing.
rows.anchor: هو القالب الحامل للقلب أو المعنى الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the resurrection sign became clear, Ezra affirmed ongoing knowledge that God can do everything, including this miracle.
rows.anchor: إن الله على كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending in God’s cause includes all good works, jihad among them; an alternative restricts the special multiplication to jihad and gives other charity only tenfold.
rows.anchor: أي في وجوه الخيرات الشاملة للجهاد وغيره وقيل : المراد الإنفاق في الجهاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative view says the verse’s seven-hundredfold multiplication applies specifically to spending in jihad, while other spending receives the ordinary tenfold reward.
rows.anchor: المراد الإنفاق في الجهاد لأنه الذي يضاعف هذه الأضعاف وأما الإنفاق في غيره فلا يضاعف كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison needs an implied genitive on one side: either their expenditure is like a grain, or the spenders are like someone sowing one grain.
rows.anchor: خبر عن المبتدأ قبله ولابد من تقدير مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A grain is generally a staple crop, especially wheat; non-food plant seed is more commonly called ḥabba with kasra.
rows.anchor: والحبة واحدة الحب وهو ما يزرع للإقتيات وأكثر إطلاقه على البر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seed is the causal occasion of growth, but God is the actual grower; the vivid comparison makes an abstract multiplication visible.
rows.anchor: وإسناد الإنبات إلى الحبة مجاز لأنها سبب للإنبات والمنبت في الحقيقة هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word sunbula is commonly analyzed with an extra nūn, from asbala meaning that grain formed ears; another analysis treats nūn as root, but the first is better known.
rows.anchor: وقيل : وزنه فعلله فالنون أصلية والأول هو المشهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may multiply this reward beyond sevenfold, as well as to seven hundred; the author favors this unrestricted reading as more beneficial.
rows.anchor: وإقتصر بعض على الأول وبعض على الثاني والتعميم أتم نفعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The degree of reward varies with the spender’s sincerity and effort and with choosing the best occasion for giving.
rows.anchor: على حسب حالهم من الإخلاص والتعب وإيقاع الإنفاق في أحسن مواقعه

rows.speaker: ابن ماجه، وابن أبي حاتم
rows.claim: A report from several Companions traces to the Prophet: each dirham sent to support God’s cause earns seven hundred; personally campaigning and spending earns seven hundred thousand on Judgment Day, then he recited the verse.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن ماجه وابن أبي حاتم عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وأبي الدرداء وأبي هريرة

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: God has stored for those who finance military campaigns treasures of mercy beyond human knowledge.
rows.anchor: وعن معاذ بن جبل إن غزاة المنفقين قد خبأ الله تعالى لهم من خزائن رحمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After accounts demonstrating resurrection, the passage turns to spending and its recompense at resurrection; similar spending passages follow the earlier account of those fleeing death and David’s fight with Goliath.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر قصة المار على القرية وقصة إبراهيم عليه الصلاة والسلام وكانا من أدل دليل على البعث ذكر ما ينفع به يوم البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single earthly seed producing seven hundred grains signals God’s power to raise the dead from their graves, since both processes involve nourishment and growth.
rows.anchor: إذ من كان قادرا على أن يخرج من حبة واحدة في الأرض سبعمائة حبة فهو قادر على أن يخرج الموتى من قبورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins by explaining the proper manner of the previously praised spending: donors must not follow gifts with reminders of favor or injury to recipients.
rows.anchor: ثم لا يتبعون ما أنفقوا ( أي إنفاقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man originally means cutting, and injury means patronizing or boasting over recipients; man precedes injury because it occurs more often.
rows.anchor: والمن عبد الإحسان وهو في الأصل القطع ومنه قوله : حبل منين أي ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word thumma signals the greater rank and distance between giving and avoiding reproach or harm; al-Intiṣāf instead reads it as prolonged persistence in avoiding them, which the author considers preferable.
rows.anchor: للتفاوت بين الإنفاق وترك المن والأذى في الرتبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Intiṣāf’s interpretation makes thumma signify enduring continued conduct, as in steadfastness after initial commitment and lasting guidance, and preserves its core sense of temporal extension.
rows.anchor: وذكر في الإنتصاف وجها آخر في ذلك وهو الدلالة على دوام الفعل المعطوف بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī, transmitting from al-Kalbī with an explicit reservation, says the verse was revealed about ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf’s large charitable contributions.
rows.anchor: والآية كما أخرج الواحدي عن كلبي والعهدة عليه نزلت في عثمان بن عفان وعبدالرحمن بن عوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān gave four thousand dirhams, half of his eight thousand savings, as a loan to God; the Prophet blessed both the gift and what he kept for his family.
rows.anchor: فقال : كان عندي ثمانية آلاف درهم فأمسكت منها لنفسي وعيالي أربعة آلاف درهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUthmān pledged to equip anyone lacking equipment on the Tabūk expedition, supplied a thousand camels with gear, and gave the Muslims his well of Rumah.
rows.anchor: أما عثمان رضي الله تعالى عنه فقال : علي جهاز من لا جهاز له في غزوة تبوك فجهز المسلمين بألف بعير

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd says he saw the Prophet praying for ʿUthmān with raised hands until dawn, after which the verse about those who spend was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سعيد الخدري : رأيت رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم رافعا يديه يدعو لعثمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that donors have their reward with their Lord is restated for emphasis and honor; omitting an expected conditional fa suggests their inner good intention merits reward in itself.
rows.anchor: من التأكيد والتشريف ما لا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise means fear and grief will be absent continuously, rather than merely denying that their absence itself will ever end.
rows.anchor: المراد بيان دوام إنتفائهما لا بيان إنتفاء دوامهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kind response to a petitioner—such as wishing God’s mercy or provision, or promising to give later—and overlooking an intrusive request are better than a gift followed by injury.
rows.anchor: أي كلام جميل يرد به السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible reading makes forgiveness God’s forgiveness of the person enduring a difficult petitioner, or the petitioner’s forgiveness of a refusal; the author rejects these as mismatched comparisons.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يحتمل أن يراد بالمغفرة مغفرة الله تعالى للمسئول بسبب تحمله ما يكره من السائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed alternatives fail because the comparison should contrast two qualities of the same person, and they imply some good in a wholly invalid harmful gift.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن الأنسب أن يكون المفضل والمفضل عليه في هذا المقام كلاهما صفتي شخص واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence confirms the instruction to avoid reproach and harm; it omits reproach because injury includes reproach and more, and the indefinite opening is licensed by qualification or coordination.
rows.anchor: والجملة مستأنفة مقررة لإعتبار ترك إتباع المن والأذى وإنما لم يذكر المن لأن الأذى يشمله وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is independent of people’s charity and commands it for their benefit; alternatively, He rejects charity mixed with reproach, or can provide the poor elsewhere so they need not endure it.
rows.anchor: عن صدقات العباد وإنما أمرهم بها لمصلحة تعود إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is forbearing: He delays punishment for reproach and injury, though their perpetrators deserve it; the ending therefore carries both promise and warning.
rows.anchor: فلا يعجل بالعقوبة على المن والإيذاء لاأنهم لا يستحقونها بسببهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct address to believers follows third-person description to strengthen the command; the charity is spoiled by either reproach or injury, with reproach usually directed to the poor.
rows.anchor: أقبل عليهم بالخطاب إثر بيان ما بين بطريق الغيبة البالغة في إيجاب العمل بموجب النهي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to interpret reproach as being directed toward God; injury is directed toward the poor recipient.
rows.anchor: المراد به المن على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that the verse appears to say either reproach or injury cancels charity, although the gift has occurred and Sunni doctrine says sins do not cancel good deeds, unlike the Muʿtazilite position.
rows.anchor: وإستشكل ابن عطية هذه الآية بأن ظاهرها يستدعي أن أجر الصدقة يبطل بأحد هذين الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer offered is that God never accepts a gift from someone He knows will reproach or hurt its recipient; some say an angel is marked not to record it, so no accepted deed is later annulled.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن الصدقة التي يعلم الله تعالى من صاحبها أنه يمن ويؤذي لا تقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That answer means do not perform the act as an invalid gift, rather than canceling a valid accepted deed; the author admits this departs from the apparent wording, though the simile partly supports it.
rows.anchor: حينئذ لا تأتوا بهذا العمل باطلا كذا قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase comparing the donor to one who spends for show may modify an implied noun for nullifying or describe the acting donors’ state; the latter supports the proposed answer because ostentation is never accepted.
rows.anchor: في محل نصب إما على أنه نعت لمصدر محذوف أي لا تبطلوها إبطالا كإبطال الذي الخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riyāʾ can be the purpose of spending or the donor’s state; its verbal form is reciprocal because the donor displays deeds and people return praise and honor.
rows.anchor: إما على أنه علة لينفق أي لأجل ريائهم

rows.speaker: الخزاعي، الشموني
rows.claim: Al-Khuzāʿī and al-Shamūnī are among those who read the first hamza of riyāʾ lightly as a yāʾ to avoid the weight of a hamza after kasra.
rows.anchor: ويجوز تخفيف الهمزة الأولى بأن تقلب ياءا فرارا من ثقل الهمزة بعد الكسرة وقد قرأ به الخزاعي والشموني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the ostentatious donor may be a believer or unbeliever, but most commentators take him as a hypocrite because he does not believe in God and the Last Day.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الموصول ما يشمل المؤمن والكافر كما قيل وغالب المفسرين على أن المراد به المنافق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣafwān is a large smooth stone, whether analyzed as a collective, a plural, or a genus noun; its thin dust is washed away by a powerful downpour.
rows.anchor: أي حجر كبير أملس وهو جمع صفوانة أو صفاء أو إسم جنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison can map stone, dust, and rain separately to the useless donor, apparent hope of reward, and ostentation, or work as one composite image; a reported view calls the composite the right reading.
rows.anchor: وهذا التشبيه يجوز أن يكون مفرقا فالنافق المنافق كالحجر في عدم الإنتفاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ostentatious donor can attain no reward or benefit from what he spent; this either explains the comparison or answers an implied question about its outcome.
rows.anchor: أي لا يجدون ثواب شيء مما أنفقوا رياءا

rows.speaker: السمين
rows.claim: Al-Samīn’s suggestion that the clause is a circumstantial modifier of the relative antecedent is judged weak.
rows.anchor: وجعلها حال من الذي كما قال : السمين مهزول من القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun may refer to the singular-form relative by meaning; alternatives include collective usage or treating man and alladhī as interchangeable, while return to the believers is dismissed.
rows.anchor: والضمير راجع إلى الموصول بإعتبار المعنى بعدما روعي لفظه إذ هو صفة لمفرد لفظا مجموع معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s statement that He does not guide the unbelieving people closes the argument and implies reproach, injury, and ostentation are traits believers must avoid.
rows.anchor: وفيه تعريض بأن كلا من الرياء والمن والأذى على الإنفاق من صفات الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending to seek God’s pleasure means giving in order to obtain His approval.
rows.anchor: أي لطلب رضاه أو طالبين له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase strengthening oneself may use min partitivally: spending engages one faculty of the self; giving both wealth and life would engage the whole self.
rows.anchor: فمن تبعيضية كما في قولهم : هز من عطفية وحرك من نشاطه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, min is origination and the omitted object is Islam or confirmation of recompense, rooted in the heart; it may also indicate proving sincerity to other believers.
rows.anchor: وقد يجعل مفعول تثبيتا محذوفا أي تثبيتا للإسلام وتحقيقا للجزاء من أصل أنفسهم وقلوبهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid’s reading tabyīnan, ‘making clear,’ supports interpreting the phrase as showing others one’s sincere faith.
rows.anchor: ويعضده قراءة مجاهد وتبيينا من أنفسهم

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī takes min to mean li, so the phrase describes steadying oneself for obedience to God; the author finds this plausible.
rows.anchor: بمعنى اللام والمعنى توطينا لأنفسهم على طاعة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending purifies the donor from miserliness and love of wealth, described as a grave disease and root of every sin.
rows.anchor: وفيه تنبيه على أن حكمة الإنفاق للمنفق تزكية للنفس عن البخل وحب المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A garden on elevated ground has especially attractive trees and wholesome fruit because its air is mild and does not stagnate densely.
rows.anchor: وأعتبر كونها في ربوة لأن أشجار الربى تكون أحسن منظرا وأزكى ثمرا للطافة هوائها

rows.speaker: ابن عامر، عاصم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read rabwa with fatḥ; most read ḍamm, Ibn ʿAbbās reads kasr, and another form is rabāwa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وعاصم بربوة بالفتح والباقون بالضم وابن عباس بالكسر وقرئ رباوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads ḥabba, ‘grain,’ instead of janna, ‘garden.’
rows.anchor: وقرئ كمثل حبة بالحاء والباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled yield may mean repeated abundance, twice the ordinary crop after heavy rain, four times if ḍiʿf means double, or two harvests in one year.
rows.anchor: فالتثنية للتكثير أو مثلي ما كانت تثمر

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، ابن كثير، نافع
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ read the kāf in akl with sukūn as a lightened pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير ونافع بسكون الكاف تخفيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even light drizzle suffices for a good garden on high ground, so sincere spending never fails to yield reward, though sincerity, effort, love of wealth, and the recipient’s need affect its degree.
rows.anchor: والمراد أن خيرها لا يخلف على حال لجودنها وكرم منبتها ولطافة هوائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogy may be composite, matching pure growing expenditure with a pure fruitful garden under either rain, or differentiated, matching the donors and their small or great gifts with garden and rain.
rows.anchor: فهناك تشبيه حال النفقة النامية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the composite analysis the common feature is growth joined with purity; on the differentiated analysis, either the expenditure or the donor is the main comparison, and scholars prefer different constructions.
rows.anchor: وهذا من التشبيه المركب العقلي ولك أن تعتبر تشبيه حال أولئك عند الله تعالى بالجنة على الربوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees every deed and rewards the sincere while warning the ostentatious giver who seeks the gaze of those whose view cannot help, instead of God’s decisive sight.
rows.anchor: فيجازي كلا من المخلص والمرائي بما هو أعلم به ففي الجملة ترغيب للأول وترهيب للثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening asks whether anyone would love this outcome; the hamza is reproachful, and a report says ʿUmar read yuḥibbu, ‘would love.’
rows.anchor: أي أيحب أحدكم وكذلك قرأ عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden is centered on palms and grapes, the most valuable core species, without excluding others; the Qur’an names the palm tree itself but grape fruit, perhaps because the palm is wholly useful.
rows.anchor: على معنى أنهما الركن والأصل فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Palm trees are analyzed either as a collective plural or a collective noun; grapes is the plural of ʿinaba, while ʿinbāʾ is a feminine-marked form that does not decline.
rows.anchor: وقيل : جمع نخل وهو إسم جنس جمعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression janna may mean the dense trees themselves or land containing them; the first is more fitting because rivers run beneath it without supplying an omitted ‘trees.’
rows.anchor: والأول أنسب بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘he has therein of every fruit,’ the prepositional phrase can be a fronted predicate, while ‘of every fruit’ describes an omitted provision or fruit; min may be extra under al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: الظرف الأول في محل رفع جبر مقدم والثاني حال من الضمير المستتر في الخبر والثالث نعت لمبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Every fruit’ means many kinds rather than literally all; reading fruit as benefits or as general after the two named kinds is also discussed, with the latter rejected.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد بالثمرات العموم بل إنما هو الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden owner is struck by old age, a more forceful expression than simply being old; the circumstantial clause highlights his urgent need and inability to restore his livelihood.
rows.anchor: أي أثر فيه علو السن والشيخوخة وهو أبلغ من كبر

rows.speaker: الفراء، أبو حيان
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows the coordinated past tense to represent a future result; Abū Ḥayyān objects that this makes the old age part of the wish, which the author finds unconvincing to dismiss.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الواو للعطف ووضع الماضي موضع المضارع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The weak offspring are dependents unable to earn a living; ḍuʿafāʾ is a plural of ḍaʿīf, and a variant reads ḍiʿāf.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال من الضمير في أصابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An iʿṣār is a rotating whirlwind, descending or rising, generated when competing air currents collide; it can grow strong enough to uproot trees or snatch boats.
rows.anchor: أي ريح تستدير على نفسها وتكون مثل المنارة وتسمى الزوبعة وهي قد تكون هابطة وقد تكون صاعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire-bearing whirlwind is named and described for its rhetorical force; it may wrap like a twisted cloth or squeeze clouds and passing bodies, and tanwīn magnifies the fire.
rows.anchor: وتذكير الضمير لإعتبار التذكير فيه وإنما سمى ذلك الهواء إعصارا لأنه يلتف كما يلتف الثوب المعصور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets iʿṣār as any violent wind and its fire as the scorching samūm.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أن الإعصار الريح الشديدة مطلقا وأن المراد من النار السموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This image portrays the grief of a donor whose good deeds are nullified just when old and needy on Judgment Day, like an elderly parent losing the family’s garden.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما روي عن السدي تمثيل حال من ينفق ويضم إلى إنفاقه ما يحبطه في الحسرة والأسف إذا كان يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports that ʿUmar asked about the parable; Ibn ʿAbbās explained a formerly righteous person who, near death and most in need of a good ending, commits sins and burns his deeds, impressing ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبد بن حميد عن عطاء أن عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A version transmitted by al-Bukhārī, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Jarīr, and others has ʿUmar ask the Companions about the verse and Ibn ʿAbbās describe a rich obedient person corrupted by Satan until his deeds burn.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية البخاري والحاكم وابن جرير وجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn ʿAbbās interpretation is stronger than limiting the parable to charity invalidated by reproach or ostentation, since he is the Qur’an’s interpreter and ʿUmar accepted it.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن هذا لا يدفع أحسنية ذلك لا سيما وقد قاله ترجمان القرآن وإرتضاه الأمير المحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are explained clearly so people may reflect on their lessons, take heed, and act accordingly.
rows.anchor: أي كي تتفكروا فيها وتعتبروا بما تضمنته من العبر وتعملوا بموجبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, people should direct thought to what perishes in this world and what endures in the next, thereby giving and seeking the afterlife rather than grieving over worldly loss.
rows.anchor: أو لعلكم تعملون أفكاركم فيما يفنى ويضمحل من الدنيا وفيما هو باق لكم في الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command covers good or lawful earnings, including currency, trade goods, and livestock; earthly produce forms a separate category.
rows.anchor: أي مكسوبكم من النقد وعروض التجارة والمواشي

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a report from Ibn Jarīr, ʿAlī says earned good things are gold and silver, while God’s produce includes grain, dates, and everything subject to zakat.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating min marks two independently valid sources of giving, or serves for emphasis, which the author regards as more likely.
rows.anchor: في المعطوف لأن كلا من المتعاطفين نوع مستقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause describes what may be given, after the passage explained the basic obligation and manner of spending.
rows.anchor: والجملة لبيان حال ما ينفق منه إثر بيان أصل الإنفاق وكيفيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayammamū means deliberately aim at something; one of its two initial tāʾs is dropped, and reading variants by ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn ʿAbbās carry the same meaning.
rows.anchor: أي تقصدوا وأصله تتيمموا بتاءين فحذفت إحداهما تخفيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khabīth means defective or poor quality and functions as a substantive adjective; preposing ‘from it you spend’ restricts attention to their practice of donating inferior goods.
rows.anchor: أي الردئ وهو كالطيب من الصفات الغالبة التى لا تذكر موصوفاتها

rows.speaker: عبيدة السلماني
rows.claim: ʿUbayda al-Salmānī says ʿAlī explained that the verse concerns obligatory zakat: harvesters saved their good dates and gave poor-quality dates to the collector.
rows.anchor: سألت عليا كرم الله تعالى وجهه عن هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase says donors would take such inferior goods only by overlooking their defects; accepting them is like closing one’s eyes or tolerating a flaw.
rows.anchor: أنكم لستم بآخذيه في وقت من الأوقات أو بوجه من الوجوه

rows.speaker: الزهرى، قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī intensifies the mīm or varies its vowel; Qatāda reads a passive form meaning donors are made to overlook the defects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهرى تغمضوا بتشديد الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parse making an as-clause a circumstantial modifier conflicts with Sībawayh, and al-Farrāʾ’s conditional reading should be rejected; a remote alternative divides the phrase into a rebuke and question.
rows.anchor: هنا شرطية لأن معناه إن أغمضتم أخذتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no gifts and ordered them for donors’ benefit; giving inferior goods shows ignorance of His greatness, while gratitude entails selecting good gifts.
rows.anchor: وفي الأمر بأن يعلموا ذلك مع ظهور علمهم به توبيخ لهم على ما يصنعون من إعطاء الخبيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is used to argue that land produce, even small crops and vegetables, owes zakat; a tenant farmer pays it, and a creditor need not accept defective goods instead of sound payment.
rows.anchor: وإحتج بالآية على وجوب زكاة قليل ما تخرجه الأرض وكثيره حتى البقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse explains why people target inferior goods: Satan frightens donors that spending good wealth will make them poor; the threat is presented as certain, as if caused by Satan himself.
rows.anchor: إستئناف لبيان سبب تيمم الخبيث في الإنفاق وتوهين شأنه والوعد في أصل وضعه لغة شائع في الخير والشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some claim the threat is actually a promise of good because poverty caused by giving is virtuous; the author says this is far from the Qur’an’s intent.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من زعم أن إستعمال الوعد هنا في الخير حسب الإستعمال الشائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faqr has several transmitted vocalizations, and its root refers to breaking the vertebrae of the back.
rows.anchor: وقرئ الفقر بالضم والسكون وبفتحتين وضمتين وكلها لغات في الفقر وأصله كسر فقار الظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disgraceful command is chiefly stinginess and withholding charity; Arabs called a miser fāḥish, as in Kaʿb’s verse, while broader sins or adultery are also suggested.
rows.anchor: أي الخصلة الفحشاء وهي البخل وترك الصدقات

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb’s line uses fāḥish to describe a man who is not lewd or miserly at home or in company, illustrating the word’s application to miserliness.
rows.anchor: قال كعب : أخي يا أخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ‘commands’ metaphorically means incites and urges, a transferred metaphor; the warning comes first because once fear of poverty settles, Satan dominates with commands.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالأمر بذلك الإغراء والحث عليه ففى الكلام إستعارة مصرحة تبعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises forgiveness and bounty through the Prophet; forgiveness may cover sins or, according to Qatāda, the stinginess just condemned, while bounty is provision or replacement.
rows.anchor: على لسان نبيكم صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains bounty as provision or compensation, pairing forgiveness for the afterlife with worldly benefit; a hadith has two angels pray each morning for spenders’ replacement and misers’ loss.
rows.anchor: أي رزقا وخلفا وهو المروي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others place both forgiveness and bounty in the afterlife, with forgiveness first because removing harm precedes granting benefit; the author links this to 3:185.
rows.anchor: تقديم الأول حينئذ لتقدم التخلية على التحلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second coordinated noun omits a quality recoverable from the first; God is expansive in mercy and bounty and knows what donors give to repay it.
rows.anchor: والله وسع ( بالرحمة والفضل ( عليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author points to a parallel verse for this divine statement about recompense.
rows.anchor: ومثلها في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable shows that wealth cannot help disbelievers; children need no separate explanation because unbelieving children share judgment, while believing children may oppose their parents and abandon them on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: كالدليل لعدم إغناء الأموال ولعل عدم بيان إغناء الأولاد ظاهر لأنهم إن كانوا كفاراوهو الظاهركان حكمهم حكمهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The relative mā represents all forms of disbelievers’ expenditure, whatever their kind; other views restrict it to anti-Prophetic spending generally, Quraysh at Badr and Uḥud, or subordinate Jews funding corrupt scholars.
rows.anchor: والمراد تمثيل جميع صدقات الكفار ونفقاتهم كيف كانتوهو المروى عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rīḥ here is singular; ṣirr can mean severe cold according to Ibn ʿAbbās and others, while al-Zajjāj says a fiery blaze was present in the wind.
rows.anchor: أي برد شديد قاله إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما وجماعة

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others explain ṣirr as intense cold; a separate explanation makes it fire’s flare.
rows.anchor: أي برد شديد قاله إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما وجماعة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says ṣirr means a flame of fire that was contained in the wind.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج الصرصوت لهيب النار وقد كانت في تلك الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating ṣirr as a cold wind within a wind needs strained explanation; he favors its usual sense of cold, while recorded alternatives derive it from sound or a stormy cry but lack established usage.
rows.anchor: وعليه يكون معنى النظم ريح فيها ريح باردة وهو كما ترى محتاج إلى التوجيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some parse ṣirr as an adjective with an omitted noun, but deleting the noun is unfamiliar; another view takes the word as wind’s own sound, which is unattested.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه صفة بمعنى بارد إلا أن موصوفه محذوف أي برد بارد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rīḥ derives from a wāw-root and has plural forms arwāḥ and aryāḥ; the singular may also appear as rīḥa, like dār and dāra.
rows.anchor: والريح واحدة الرياح وفي الصحاح والأرياح وقد تجمع على أرواح لأن أصلها الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tradition says one wind is associated with punishment and plural winds with mercy, prompting the prayer that it be winds rather than a single wind.
rows.anchor: وأفرد الريح لما في البحر أنها مختصة بالعذاب والجمع مختص بالرحمة ولذلك روى اللهمأجعلها رياحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The field’s owners wronged themselves by unbelief and disobedience, so God’s destruction was especially dreadful; alternatively, the phrase says only unbelievers lose both worldly and afterlife benefit, while others may be rewarded for patience.
rows.anchor: قوم ظلموا أنفسهم بالكفر والمعاصي فباؤا بغضب من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says they wronged themselves by planting in the wrong place or season; the crop was destroyed utterly, as punishment or correction for misplacing what belonged elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد ظلموا أنفسهم بأن زرعوا في غير موضع الزراعة وفي غير وقتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison is composite, and its central point is waste and meager yield; a composite comparison need not place the thing named after the particle as the exact counterpart.
rows.anchor: وهذا من التشبيه المركب الذي توجد فيه الزبدة من الخلاصة والمجموع ولا يلزم فيه أن يكون ما يلي الأداة هو المشبه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses compare the destruction of spending with wind destroying a field, or the spending itself with a destructive wind; a differentiated reading maps God’s destruction and the expenditure separately.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد مثل إهلاك ما ينفقون كمثل إهلاك ريح أو مثل ما ينفقون كمهلك ريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The frozen wind makes the crop worthless, mirroring God’s rendering their deeds scattered; the focus is negligible yield and loss.
rows.anchor: والوجه عند كونه مركبا قلة الجدوى والضياع ويجوز أن يكون من التشبيه المفرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘God did not wrong them’ may refer to the spenders, whose wasted expenditure was inappropriate, or to the field’s people, who deserved its destruction.
rows.anchor: الضمير إما للمنفقين أي ما ظلمهم بضياع نفقاتهم التي أنفقوها على غير الوجه اللائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A doubled-lām reading of lākin makes ‘themselves’ its subject and ‘they wrong’ its predicate with an omitted object; the light reading also omits the object, not fronting ‘themselves.’
rows.anchor: وقريء ( ولكن ) بالتشديد على أن أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shān pronoun would ordinarily not be omitted outside poetry; a poetic line about love is offered as evidence, though the author regards the analysis as difficult.
rows.anchor: وأسمها ضمير الشأن لأنه لا يحذف إلا في الشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting ‘themselves’ serves the verse ending, not exclusivity; the present tense indicates repeated, continuing self-wronging.
rows.anchor: وتقديم أنفسهم على الفعل للفاصلة لا للحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse corrects the miser’s belief that hoarding is good and follows the preceding warning about being allowed respite; alternatively it continues the call to give lives by urging giving wealth.
rows.anchor: بيان لحال البخل وسوء عاقبته وتخطئة لأهله في دعواهم خيريته حسب بيان حال الإملاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Describing the hoarded wealth as God’s gift magnifies the wrong: receiving it from divine bounty should prompt its use in God’s cause.
rows.anchor: وإيراد ما بخلوا به بعنوان إيتاء الله تعالى إياه من فضله للمبالغة في بيان سوء صنيعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first object of ḥasiba is omitted though the verb seeks two objects; an objection says its double grammatical demand should prevent deletion, but deletion of kāna’s predicate shows that inference fails.
rows.anchor: وفعل الحسبان مسند إلى الموصول والمفعول الأول محذوف لدلالة الصلة عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī permits omitting an object of ḥasiba only when subject and objects are semantically one; the author rejects this as the governing rule and says contextual indication is decisive.
rows.anchor: ونقل الطيبي عن صاحب الكشاف أن حذف أحد مفعولى حسب إنما يجوز إذا كان فاعل حسب ومفعولاه شيئا واحدا في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Object omission depends on a clear contextual clue: it is allowed where indicated and not where it is absent, regardless of semantic identity.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن مدار صحة الحذف القرينة فمتى وجدت جاز الحذف ومتى لم توجد لم يجز

rows.speaker: عصام الدين، أبو البقاء
rows.claim: A proposed parse treats huwa as an accusative pronoun or emphatic pronoun, but the author calls it strained and cites al-Durr al-Maṣūn calling that analysis an error.
rows.anchor: والقول بأن هو ضمير رفع أستعير في مكان المنصوب وهو راجع إلى البخل أو الإيتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead takes huwa as a separator between the two objects of ḥasiba; the alternative addressed reading requires the first object to mean the hoarding of those who withhold zakat.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه ضمير فصل بين مفعولي حسب لا توكيد للمظهر كما توهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the addressed reading, the first object is the relative phrase understood as their hoarding of what God gave, and the second is ‘good’; an omitted genitive is needed.
rows.anchor: وهو خلاف الطاهر نعم إنه متعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says what they hoard is evil for them, then explains the evil through their being encircled by it on Judgment Day; the extra sīn intensifies the threat.
rows.anchor: سيطوقون ما بخلوا به يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A hadith in al-Bukhārī says that one who fails to pay zakat on divinely granted wealth will meet a bald two-marked snake that coils around him, grips his jaw, and says it is his wealth and treasure.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Another prophetic report says a relative who refuses a petitioner from God’s bounty will meet a hellish snake on Judgment Day that licks its lips and coils around him.
rows.anchor: وأخرج غير واحد عن النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī says the hoarded wealth itself will become a collar of fire around the hoarder’s neck.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عبدالرزاق وغيره عن إبراهيم النخعي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets the threat as forcing misers to produce an equal sum on Judgment Day, which they will be unable to do.
rows.anchor: كما قال مجاهد : سيكلفون أن يأتوا بمثل

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads it figuratively: they will bear the consequence of their miserliness like a collar, with a deleted ‘consequence’ implied.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم : سيلزمون وبال ما بخلوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent literal warning is the majority position and the verse apparently concerns those withholding zakat, as reports from al-Ṣādiq, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shaʿbī, al-Suddī, and others indicate.
rows.anchor: وكيفما كان فالآية نزلت في مانعي الزكاة كما روى ذلك عن الصادق وإبن مسعود والشعبي والسدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report says the verse concerns People of the Book who concealed the Torah’s description and prophecy of Muḥammad; their withheld bounty is the Torah, and the collar may be fire or the consequence of concealment.
rows.anchor: وأخرج إبن جرير وإبن أبي حاتم عن إبن عباس أنها نزلت في أهل الكتاب الذين كتموا صفة رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the People of the Book interpretation, the passage returns to the discussion leading into the Battle of Uḥud; many later verses in the sūra also concern them.
rows.anchor: وعليه يكون هذا عودا إلى ما أنجر منه الكلام إلى قصة أحد وذلك هو شرح أحوال أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone inherits all transferable possessions and states in heaven and earth, including prophetic missions; therefore misers withhold from the true owner what belongs to Him.
rows.anchor: لله تعالى وحده لا لأحد غيره إستقلالا أو إشتراكا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains the inheritance literally: God ends the inhabitants’ lives, leaving heaven and earth and all they contain without another owner.
rows.anchor: أي إن الله تعالى يفنى أهلهما فيبقيان بما فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows their withholding and miserliness; naming Him directly builds awe, while shifting to direct address intensifies the threat; Nāfiʿ and others read second-person, the rest third-person.
rows.anchor: والله بما تعملون من المنع والبخل خبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation of heaven and earth confirms and proves the preceding statement; the verse opens with emphatic inna and no coordinating conjunction to signal its importance.
rows.anchor: تأكيد لما قبله وإقامة دليل عليه ولذا لم يعطف وأتى بكلمة إن إعتناءا بتحقق مضمون الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day alternate as the sun rises and sets, itself swimming through the sea of God’s power according to divine will.
rows.anchor: أي تعاقبها ومجيء كل منهما خلف الآخر بحسب طلوع الشمس وغروبها التابعين لسباحتها في بحر قدرته سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the heavens move while earth remains still conflicts with the majority Sunni view that the heavens are stationary and stars move by God’s decree; he identifies the former as the philosophers’ popular position.
rows.anchor: مخالف لما ذهب إليه جمهور أهل السنة من المحدثين وغيرهم من سكون السموات وتحرك النجوم أنفسها

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī says the heavens are stationary spheres in which stars move measured courses, creating musical sounds through adjacent air; astronomers calculate motions and eclipses correctly but mistake their proposed physical ordering for reality.
rows.anchor: إن الله سبحانه جعل هذه السموات ساكنة وخلق فيها نجوما تسبح بها وجعل لها في سباحتها حركات مقدرة
